paragraph: Sita donned her bark robes like a woebegone waif, though consort to the mighty Ikshvaku. "Blamed be Dasaratha" condemned the people of Ayodhya as they wept at the injustice. Hearing the heart-rending sounds of grief, Dasaratha no longer cared for his honor, his fame or his life. Sighing deeply he said, "How can a dainty princess inhabit the jungles? What harm has this virtuous daughter of a virtuous king done to warrant her banishment? Though wrested out of me against my will, the barbarous command I have issued makes me unfit to live. Kaikeyi! Blind to your devious designs I granted you the boons. Now by unscrupulously exiling Rama you commit an act that will destroy you, as a bamboo bloom destroys the very bamboo out of which it was born. Your desire to see Sita clothed in bark robes will cast you in hell. Sinful woman! For what fault of hers do you punish her so and what harm has Rama done?" To Dasaratha who could not control his grief Rama said, "Father, Kausalya that virtuous queen of yours, though immersed in sorrow does not blame you. Never has she suffered any hardships and you are her only refuge, do comfort her. She needs all your kindness and support, to bear the pain of my separation from her. Protect her, because pining for me, she may even die.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Sita wears the ascetic robes, eliciting widespread grief and condemnation from the people of Ayodhya. Dasaratha, consumed by despair, blames Kaikeyi for the injustice and expresses his own desire to die. Rama, witnessing his father's profound grief, attempts to console him by emphasizing the need to care for Queen Kausalya, who will be devastated by his absence.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: This passage showcases the immense suffering caused by injustice and the collective grief of a devoted populace. It highlights Dasaratha's profound guilt and despair, contrasting with Rama's selflessness in prioritizing his mother's well-being even in his own moment of departure. It emphasizes duty, compassion, and the enduring pain of separation.
Outcome/Resolution: Sita's donning of the bark robes intensifies the collective grief and condemnation of Ayodhya, plunging Dasaratha into deeper despair and guilt, leading him to wish for death. Rama intervenes, not to reverse the situation, but to redirect his father's focus towards caring for Kausalya, thereby attempting to manage the cascading emotional fallout. The immediate outcome is Dasaratha's continued grief but also Rama's selfless act of trying to ensure his mother's well-being, setting the stage for the direct departure into exile while emphasizing the ongoing emotional burden on the family.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.stress Management: Coping failure, Overwhelmed, Emotional collapse, Compassionate intervention, Supportive coping

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Shoka (Grief - The pervasive sorrow of Sita, Dasaratha, the people, and Kausalya is a central manifestation of Shoka)
Adharma (Unrighteousness - Dasaratha condemns Kaikeyi's actions as 'barbarous' and 'unscrupulous,' highlighting their deviation from dharma)
Karma Phala (Fruits of Action - Dasaratha implies Kaikeyi's actions will bring about her own destruction, like the bamboo bloom, a karmic consequence)
Dharma (Righteous Duty - Rama's plea for Dasaratha to care for Kausalya emphasizes his dharma towards his mother, even amidst his own suffering)
Moha (Delusion - Dasaratha laments being 'blind to your devious designs,' suggesting a form of Moha that allowed Kaikeyi's plans to succeed)
Tyaga (Sacrifice - Dasaratha's readiness to abandon his life mirrors Rama's sacrifice, though born of despair rather than duty)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: The scene is steeped in 'Shoka' (grief) as Sita dons ascetic robes and the people condemn the 'Adharma' (unrighteousness) that led to Rama's exile. Dasaratha, overcome by guilt and despair, foresees Kaikeyi's 'Karma Phala' (consequences) and wishes for death. Rama, despite his own pain, exemplifies 'Dharma' by urging his father to uphold his duty of comforting Kausalya, preventing further 'Shoka' for her.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, this passage vividly portrays the profound low mood, sadness, and feelings of hopelessness engulfing Dasaratha, leading to a complete failure of stress management and intense grief and loss. He is consumed by guilt and shame. Sita's appearance symbolizes her own deep sadness. Rama, however, despite his personal suffering, demonstrates remarkable emotional regulation and engages in compassionate stress management by prioritizing his mother Kausalya's emotional well-being, highlighting the complex relationship challenges and the critical need for familial support during crisis.
